stories.title: A reanalysis of supernova observational data suggests the possibility that 'the expansion of the universe is not accelerating.'
stories.description: The prevailing theory has been that 'the universe is continuously expanding, and its expansion is accelerating.' However, a research team from India's Tata Research Institute and the University of Oxford in the UK used a catalog containing observational data from over 1,700 supernovae to examine whether they could find evidence to support the 'accelerated expansion' of the universe. Their findings revealed that 'the expansion may not be accelerating.' Pantheon+ supernovae corrected for progenitor age indicate the universe is decelerating | Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society https://academic.oup.com/mnras/article/549/3/stag844/8701424 Analysis of supernova data questions evidence for cosmic acceleration | University of Oxford Department of Physics https://www.physics.ox.ac.uk/news/analysis-supernova-data-questions-evidence-cosmic-acceleration Dark energy debunked? Cosmic acceleration may be an illusion | ScienceDaily https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260907201600.htm One clue to studying the expansion of the universe is ' Type Ia supernovae ,' which are produced when white dwarfs explode. The intrinsic brightness of a Type Ia supernova can be estimated by observing how its color and brightness change over time, and by comparing its intrinsic brightness with its perceived brightness from Earth, the distance from Earth to the supernova can be determined. Furthermore, the phenomenon in which the wavelength of light stretches due to the expansion of the universe is called ' redshift .' Since the distance to a supernova predicted from the redshift differs depending on whether the expansion of the universe is accelerating or decelerating, we can investigate how the universe has expanded by comparing it with the distance determined from the brightness of the supernova. In the standard model of cosmology, it is believed that an unknown ' dark energy ' is accelerating the expansion of the universe. A research team led by Professor Emeritus Subir Sarkar focused on the possibility that the intrinsic brightness of a supernova may vary depending on the age of the star before the explosion. Previous studies have reported that, even when considering the changes in the color and brightness of the supernova's light, supernovae that occur in galaxies with a younger average age of stars tend to be dimmer. The authors of the previous studies interpreted this trend as being due to the fact that the younger the star before the explosion, the dimmer the supernova becomes. If we assume that a supernova, which is actually faint, is 'brighter than it actually is,' we might overestimate the distance to the supernova by thinking that it appears faint from Earth simply because it is 'far away.' Since this distance estimate also affects the estimation of the expansion of the universe, Sarkar et al. investigated whether it can still be said that 'the expansion of the universe is accelerating' even after considering the difference in the brightness of supernovae due to the age of the star before the explosion. The 'Pantheon+' catalog used by the research team for their analysis contains 1,701 data points recording changes in brightness for 1,550 Type Ia supernovae. To eliminate differences in supernova brightness due to the age of the pre-explosion star, the research team corrected the brightness data of supernovae selected from the catalog. The correction calculations used the average pre-explosion star age estimated for each redshift in previous studies. According to Sarkar et al., if the dark energy assumed in the standard cosmological model is accelerating the expansion of the universe, then the acceleration should not be biased towards any particular direction. Therefore, in their analysis, they separated the changes in the expansion of the universe that are common to all directions from the differences in expansion depending on the direction of observation. When the research team corrected the supernova's brightness according to the age of the star before the explosion, the expansion change common to all directions showed a deceleration. In other words, it was estimated that the universe as a whole is continuing to expand, but at a slower pace. On the other hand, there was still a tendency for expansion to appear to accelerate in certain directions, and its intensity remained almost unchanged compared to before brightness correction. The research team believes that the movement of the Earth, the observation site, may be influencing these differences depending on the direction. The Milky Way galaxy, which includes the Earth and the Sun, is moving along with the surrounding galaxies in addition to the movement associated with the expansion of the universe. Since the Earth is also moving along with the Milky Way galaxy, the location from which supernovae are observed is also moving. According to Sarkar, the tendency for the expansion of the universe to appear to be accelerating is stronger in the direction in which these galaxies are moving, and weaker for distant supernovae. Sarkar and his colleagues stated that their analysis did not yield evidence that the entire universe is undergoing accelerated expansion, and they questioned the conventional idea that this acceleration can be explained by dark energy. However, there is disagreement as to whether it is necessary to correct the brightness of supernovae according to the age of the star before the explosion. In conventional analysis, the brightness of a supernova is corrected by considering the total mass of the stars in the galaxy to which the supernova belongs. Phil Wiseman and his colleagues at the University of Southampton applied this correction and examined the previous research that Sarkar et al. used as the basis for the correction, and they found that there was no clear relationship between the brightness of a supernova and the age of the stars in the galaxy. From these results, Wiseman et al. argue that the conventional correction can take into account the differences in supernova brightness related to the age of the stars in the galaxy. Furthermore, Wiseman and his colleagues pointed out that the average age of stars in a galaxy does not directly reflect the age of stars that exploded as supernovae, and concluded from these findings that 'the evidence supporting the accelerating expansion of the universe remains unshaken.' Sarkar and his colleagues also addressed this objection in their paper, acknowledging that the relationship between the age of a star before its explosion and the brightness of a supernova is still a subject of debate. Sarkar and his colleagues plan to verify their findings using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's wide-area observation project, the ' Spatiotemporal Legacy Survey ,' which is expected to observe hundreds of thousands of supernovae.
